A Wrinkle in Time, Madeleine L'Engle's science-fiction adventure published in nineteen sixty-two, which won the Newbery Medal in nineteen sixty-three. Meg Murry is searching for her missing physicist father, who has been trapped by a malevolent force called the Black Thing while working on a secret government project. She is joined by her younger brother Charles Wallace and a neighborhood girl named Calvin. Three mysterious beings—Mrs. Whatsit, Mrs. Which, and Mrs. Who—guide them on a journey using something called tessering, which folds space to allow travel between dimensions. They travel to the planet Camazotz, which is entirely controlled by a pulsating brain called It. The novel draws on classical mythology, with references to the three Fates and to biblical and Shakespearean figures, grounding its fantasy in modern physics concepts like relativity and tesseracts. Meg's greatest weakness—her anger and willfulness—becomes her greatest strength when she uses these emotions to break free from It's mind control and confront the evil directly. Her journey is as much spiritual and emotional as it is physical. She must accept herself and her family to save them. The novel challenged conventional children's literature by embracing philosophical complexity and ambiguous characters, and it established L'Engle's reputation as a pioneering writer of idea-driven fiction for young readers.
